LESSON 1 OF 4·Understand the web

Web Application Security Fundamentals

A practical introduction to web application security: assets, users, trust boundaries, attack surface, and the difference between a bug and a security vulnerability.

Beginner20 min
Why this matters

Web application security is the practice of designing, building, testing, and operating web applications so that untrusted users cannot cross security boundaries they are not authorized to cross. Identify important assets, identify who can influence each request, map trust boundaries, and verify every security-sensitive decision on the server. A web bug becomes a security issue when it lets an untrusted party violate confidentiality, integrity, authentication, authorization, or availability.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • Start with the application model: browser or client → web server → application logic → database or internal service.
  • Map assets and actions: accounts, personal data, administrative functions, files, payments, tokens, and other sensitive operations.
  • Treat browser-controlled values, cookies, headers, URL parameters, request bodies, and client-side JavaScript as potentially attacker-controlled.
  • Find the security decision: is this user logged in, can this user edit this record, or is this value safe to pass to another interpreter?
  • Verify the decision at the trusted server-side boundary. Hiding a button in the browser is not an authorization control.

The background

Web security evolved from simple server-rendered pages into distributed applications with browsers, APIs, databases, CDNs, identity providers, third-party JavaScript, and cloud services. OWASP Top 10:2025 is an awareness baseline rather than a complete security standard; OWASP recommends ASVS when teams need verifiable application-security requirements.

Real-world examples

  • OWASP Top 10:2025 puts Broken Access Control at A01 and Authentication Failures at A07, showing how central identity and authorization are to application security.
  • Modern applications combine multiple trust boundaries: browser state, reverse proxies, application servers, databases, object storage, and third-party services. A security control is useful only if the component making the final decision actually trusts the data it uses.

What to look for

  • List sensitive assets and privileged actions before testing.
  • Identify every user-controlled input and where it is consumed.
  • Check whether authentication, authorization, validation, and security-sensitive business rules are enforced server-side.
  • Compare what the UI allows with what the underlying HTTP endpoints actually accept.
  • Look for inconsistent security controls between similar endpoints, methods, roles, or application states.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Key takeaways

  • Use a documented threat model and explicit trust boundaries.
  • Centralize authentication and authorization decisions where practical.
  • Deny access by default for protected resources and fail securely.
  • Validate and normalize security-sensitive input at the point of use.
  • Log important authentication and authorization failures without leaking secrets.
  • Use OWASP ASVS when you need a testable security-requirements baseline rather than relying on the Top 10 alone.
